title: The Concubine Who Invented Paper Money
event_summary: In 1024, the Song Dynasty government officially issued the world's first state-backed paper currency, called jiaozi, in Chengdu, Sichuan Province. This followed decades of private paper notes created by merchant guilds in the region, who found that hauling heavy iron coins across vast trade routes was destroying commerce. A group of sixteen wealthy Sichuan merchants had pooled their assets to guarantee the notes, but after fraud and defaults, the prefect Xue Tian supervised the transfer of issuance to the state, creating a dedicated Bureau of Exchange to print, regulate, and back the currency with government reserves.
why_forgotten: Western economic histories long credited European banking families of Renaissance Italy with pioneering financial instruments, and the Eurocentric framing of capitalism's origins obscured China's two-century head start on paper money. The Song Dynasty's eventual hyperinflation crisis under later rulers also made the innovation seem like a cautionary failure rather than a revolutionary breakthrough, discouraging celebratory accounts.
why_it_matters: Every banknote, digital transaction, and central banking policy in the modern world descends conceptually from this moment when a government first declared that printed paper, backed by trust and reserves rather than intrinsic metal value, could function as money. The debates the Song court had about money supply, counterfeiting, and inflation are eerily identical to those central banks navigate today, making 11th-century Sichuan the birthplace of modern monetary economics.
